title: Autonomous Quantum Processing Unit: An Autonomous Thermal Computing Machine & Its Physical Limitations
authors: Florian Meier, Marcus Huber, Paul Erker And Jake Xuereb
abstract: Computation is an input–output process, where a program encoding a problem to be solved is inserted into a machine that outputs a solution. Quantum computation conventionally relies on classical, external control outside the quantum computer to execute a program, obscuring computational and thermodynamic resources required. To understand the fundamental limits of computation, however, it is pivotal to work with a fully self-contained description of a quantum computation modeling the resources on the same footing as the computation itself. By developing a framework that we dub the autonomous Quantum Processing Unit (aQPU) we model quantum computation in the framework of autonomous thermal machines. Consisting of an internal quantum timekeeping mechanism, instruction register and memory system the aQPU allows investigating relationships between thermodynamic cost, complexity, speed and fidelity of a desired quantum computation.
tldr: The paper introduces an autonomous Quantum Processing Unit (aQPU) as a thermal machine that self-contains timekeeping, instruction, and memory, enabling study of thermodynamic costs of quantum computation.
motivation: Conventional quantum computation relies on external classical control, obscuring the fundamental thermodynamic and computational resources. A fully self-contained model is needed to understand the physical limits of computation.
method: The authors develop a framework modeling quantum computation as an autonomous thermal machine, incorporating an internal quantum clock, instruction register, and memory system, and analyze its thermodynamic properties.
result: The aQPU framework allows investigation of relationships between thermodynamic cost, complexity, speed, and fidelity of quantum computations, revealing trade-offs and fundamental limits.
conclusion: The aQPU provides a unified platform to study the physical resources required for quantum computation, bridging quantum thermodynamics and computer science.

title: Geometric Speed Limit Of State Preparation And Curved Control Spaces
authors: Maximilian Goll And Robert H. Jonsson
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2160 (2026).

The preparation of quantum many-body systems faces the difficulty that in a realistic scenario only few control parameters of the system may be accessible. In this context, an interesting connection between the energy fluctuations during state preparation and its geometric length as measured by the Fubini-Study metric was discussed by Bukov et al. in 2019 [5]. An inspiring conjecture lower bounding the energy fluctuations by the minimal geometric length of all accessible state preparation protocols was put forward together with supporting examples and numerical evidence. However, we here show that the conjecture does not hold but can be violated if the accessible parameter space has extrinsic curvature, when embedded into the space of all dynamically accessible states. We illustrate this by a number of generic qubit, qutrit and harmonic oscillator systems.

.
tldr: This paper disproves a conjecture linking energy fluctuations to geometric length in state preparation, showing violations due to curved control spaces.
motivation: Understanding fundamental speed limits in quantum state preparation is crucial for quantum control and thermodynamics. The conjecture by Bukov et al. suggested a lower bound on energy fluctuations via geometric length, but its validity was uncertain.
method: The authors analyze the geometry of state preparation protocols using the Fubini-Study metric and consider control spaces with extrinsic curvature. They construct counterexamples in qubit, qutrit, and harmonic oscillator systems.
result: They demonstrate that the conjectured bound can be violated when the accessible parameter space is curved, meaning energy fluctuations can be smaller than the minimal geometric length suggests.
conclusion: The geometric speed limit for state preparation is more nuanced than previously thought; extrinsic curvature of control spaces must be accounted for, which has implications for quantum thermodynamics and control.

title: From Superradiance To Superabsorption: An Exact Treatment Of Non-Markovian Cooperative Radiation
authors: Ignacio González And Ángel Rivas
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2159 (2026).

We investigate the emergence of cooperative radiation phenomena in ensembles of two-level atoms coupled to a lossy resonant cavity beyond the Markovian and mean-field approximations. By deriving a complete analytical solution for the two-emitter case and employing a numerically exact method for larger ensembles, we characterize the full transition from Markovian to non-Markovian collective dynamics for systems of up to [MATH] emitters. Our results reveal three distinct regimes: a Markovian phase exhibiting the standard superradiant burst, a non-Markovian phase featuring spontaneous superabsorption of the emitted field, and a critical regime marked by pulsed collective emission. We show that the critical spectral width separating these behaviors increases monotonically with the number of emitters, demonstrating that environmental memory effects can be enhanced by cooperativity. Finally, we find that the superradiant scaling of the peak intensity progressively degrades with increasing system size, approaching a subquadratic law in the limit of a perfect cavity. In this regime, spontaneous superabsorption emerges as a distinct manifestation of non-Markovian cooperativity.

.
tldr: This paper analytically and numerically studies non-Markovian cooperative radiation in two-level atoms coupled to a lossy cavity, revealing superabsorption and critical regimes.
motivation: Understanding cooperative radiation beyond Markovian and mean-field approximations is crucial for quantum information processing with hybrid systems.
method: The authors derive an exact analytical solution for two emitters and use a numerically exact method for larger ensembles to characterize the transition from Markovian to non-Markovian dynamics.
result: They identify three regimes: Markovian superradiance, non-Markovian superabsorption, and critical pulsed emission; superradiant peak intensity scaling degrades with system size, approaching subquadratic in the perfect cavity limit.
conclusion: Environmental memory effects can be enhanced by cooperativity, and spontaneous superabsorption is a distinct non-Markovian cooperative phenomenon.

title: Towards Unconditional Uncloneable Encryption
authors: Pierre Botteron, Anne Broadbent, Eric Culf, Ion Nechita, Clément Pellegrini, And Denis Rochette
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2157 (2026).

Uncloneable encryption is a cryptographic primitive which encrypts a classical message into a quantum ciphertext, such that two quantum adversaries are limited in their capacity of being able to simultaneously decrypt, given the key and quantum side-information produced from the ciphertext. Since its initial proposal and scheme in the random oracle model by Broadbent and Lord [TQC 2020], uncloneable encryption has developed into an important primitive at the foundation of quantum uncloneability for cryptographic primitives. Despite sustained efforts, however, the question of unconditional uncloneable encryption (and in particular of the simplest case, called an uncloneable bit) has remained elusive. Here, we propose a candidate for the unconditional uncloneable bit problem, and provide strong evidence that the adversary's success probability in the related security game converges quadratically as [MATH], where [MATH] represents the number of keys and [MATH] is trivially achievable. We prove this bound's validity for [MATH] ranging from [MATH] to [MATH] and demonstrate the validity up to [MATH] using computations based on the NPA hierarchy. We furthemore provide compelling heuristic evidence towards the general case. In addition, we prove an asymptotic upper bound of [MATH] and give a numerical upper bound of [MATH], which to our knowledge is the best-known value in the unconditional model.

.
tldr: Proposes a candidate for unconditional uncloneable encryption and provides strong evidence for its security.
motivation: Uncloneable encryption is a fundamental primitive in quantum cryptography, but unconditional security (without random oracles) has remained elusive.
method: The authors propose a scheme for uncloneable bit encryption and analyze its security using the NPA hierarchy and heuristic arguments, proving bounds on the adversary's success probability.
result: They prove a quadratic convergence bound for the adversary's success probability for up to 5 keys, and provide numerical and asymptotic upper bounds, with the best-known value in the unconditional model.
conclusion: The work provides strong evidence that unconditional uncloneable encryption is achievable, advancing the foundations of quantum cryptography.

title: A Complexity Theory For Non-local Quantum Computation
authors: Andreas Bluhm, Simon Höfer, Alex May, Mikka Stasiuk, Philip Verduyn Lunel, And Henry Yuen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2152 (2026).

Non-local quantum computation (NLQC) replaces a local interaction between two systems with a single round of communication and shared entanglement. Despite many partial results, it is known that a characterization of entanglement cost in at least certain NLQC tasks would imply significant breakthroughs in complexity theory. Here, we avoid these obstructions and take an indirect approach to understanding resource requirements in NLQC, which mimics the approach used by complexity theorists: we study the relative hardness of different NLQC tasks by identifying resource efficient reductions between them. Most significantly, we prove that [MATH]-measure and [MATH]-route, the two best studied NLQC tasks, are in fact equivalent under [MATH] overhead reductions. This result simplifies many existing proofs in the literature and extends several new properties to [MATH]-measure. For instance, we obtain sub-exponential upper bounds on [MATH]-measure for all functions, and efficient protocols for functions in the complexity class [MATH]. Beyond this, we study a number of other examples of NLQC tasks and their relationships.

.
tldr: This paper develops a complexity-theoretic framework for non-local quantum computation (NLQC), showing that two major NLQC tasks are equivalent under efficient reductions.
motivation: Characterizing the entanglement cost of NLQC tasks is known to be as hard as major complexity problems, so the authors take an indirect approach by studying relative hardness via reductions.
method: They define resource-efficient reductions between NLQC tasks and prove that the two best-studied tasks, f-measure and f-route, are equivalent under sub-exponential overhead reductions.
result: The equivalence simplifies existing proofs, yields sub-exponential upper bounds on f-measure for all functions, and provides efficient protocols for functions in the complexity class P.
conclusion: This work establishes a complexity theory for NLQC, enabling systematic comparison of tasks and revealing connections to classical complexity classes.

title: Entanglement In The Dicke Subspace
authors: Aabhas Gulati, Ion Nechita, And Clément Pellegrini
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2150 (2026).

We provide a complete mathematical theory for the entanglement of mixtures of Dicke states. These quantum states form an important subclass of bosonic states arising in the study of indistinguishable particles. We introduce a tensor-based parametrization where the diagonal entries of these states are encoded as a symmetric tensor, enabling a direct translation between entanglement properties and well-studied convex cones of tensors. Our results bridge multipartite entanglement theory with semialgebraic geometry and the theory of completely positive and copositive tensors. This dictionary maps separability to completely positive tensors, the PPT property to moment tensors, entanglement witnesses to copositive tensors, and decomposable witnesses to sum of squares tensors. We establish that PPT entanglement exists for all multipartite systems with local dimension [MATH] and [MATH] parties, disproving a recent conjecture. We also show that, for mixtures of Dicke states, the PPT condition with respect to the most balanced bipartition implies all other PPT conditions. We further connect bosonic extendibility of mixtures of Dicke states to the duals of known hierarchies for non-negative polynomials, such as the ones by Reznick and Polya. We thus provide semidefinite programming relaxations for separability and entanglement testing in the Dicke subspace.

.
tldr: Provides a complete mathematical theory for entanglement of mixtures of Dicke states, linking multipartite entanglement to convex cones of tensors.
motivation: To develop a unified framework for understanding entanglement in the important class of Dicke states, which arise in bosonic systems.
method: Introduces a tensor-based parametrization mapping separability to completely positive tensors, PPT property to moment tensors, and entanglement witnesses to copositive tensors.
result: Proves existence of PPT entanglement for all multipartite systems with local dimension ≥3 and ≥3 parties, and shows that the PPT condition for the most balanced bipartition implies all others.
conclusion: Provides semidefinite programming relaxations for separability and entanglement testing in the Dicke subspace, advancing entanglement theory.

title: Measuring Rényi Entropy With An Echo Protocol
authors: Yi-Neng Zhou, Robin Löwenberg, And Julian Sonner
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2146 (2026).

We present efficient and practical protocols to measure the second Rényi entropy, whose exponential is known as the purity. Our approach is based on expressing the purity in terms of transition probabilities generated by an echo-type forward-backward evolution sequence, making it applicable to quantum many-body systems. Notably, our approach does not rely on random-noise averaging, a feature that can be extended to protocols to measure out-of-time-order correlation functions, as we demonstrate. By way of example, we show that our protocols can be practically implemented in superconducting qubit-based platforms, as well as in cavity-QED trapped ultra-cold gases.

.
tldr: Presents efficient echo-based protocols to measure second Rényi entropy (purity) in quantum many-body systems without random-noise averaging.
motivation: Measuring Rényi entropy is crucial for characterizing entanglement and quantum correlations, but existing methods often require random averaging or are inefficient.
method: Expresses purity in terms of transition probabilities from an echo-type forward-backward evolution sequence, avoiding random-noise averaging; extends to out-of-time-order correlators.
result: Protocols are practical for superconducting qubits and cavity-QED trapped ultracold gases, demonstrated by example implementations.
conclusion: Provides a practical, noise-avoiding approach to measure purity and OTOCs, advancing experimental quantum information processing.

title: Decoupling Local Classicality From Classical Explainability: A Noncontextual Model For Bilocal Classical Theory And A Locally-classical But Contextual Theory
authors: Sina Soltani, Marco Erba, David Schmid, And John H.selby
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2142 (2026).

We construct an ontological model for the theory known as bilocal classical theory [1]. To our knowledge, this is only the second time that an ontological model has been constructed for an entire theory, rather than just for some particular scenarios within a theory. This result refutes a conjecture from [1] which suggested that there might be no local-realist ontological model for bilocal classical theory. Moreover, it is the first time that an ontological model has been constructed for a theory that fails to be locally tomographic, showing that the assumption of local tomography underpinning the structure theorem in [2] is a genuine limitation of the theorem. This demonstrates that in general there is no tension between failures of local tomography and classical explainability (i.e., generalised noncontextuality). In fact, bilocal classical theory is in many ways more simply understood via the underlying ontological model than it is within its original formulation (much as how odd-dimensional stabiliser subtheories can be more simply understood via Spekkens' toy theory). Furthermore, this result naturally leads to the question, does every locally-classical theory admit of an ontological model? By constructing a concrete counterexample, we show that this is not the case. Our findings demonstrate that there is no straightforward relationship between theories being locally-classical, and them being classically-explainable. This shows that the fundamental status of compositional properties (such as local tomography) is not a technical side-issue, but a central and unavoidable question for a coherent understanding even of classicality itself.

.
tldr: Constructs an ontological model for bilocal classical theory, refuting a conjecture and showing that local classicality does not imply classical explainability.
motivation: To understand the relationship between local tomography, local classicality, and generalized noncontextuality, and to test whether every locally-classical theory admits an ontological model.
method: Constructs an explicit ontological model for bilocal classical theory using a hidden variable framework, and then provides a counterexample of a locally-classical but contextual theory.
result: Bilocal classical theory has a local-realist ontological model, contrary to a previous conjecture; not all locally-classical theories are classically explainable.
conclusion: Local tomography is a genuine limitation of structure theorems, and the relationship between local classicality and classical explainability is not straightforward.

title: Measurement Incompatibility And Quantum Steering Via Linear Programming
authors: Lucas E. A. Porto, Sébastien Designolle, Sebastian Pokutta, And Marco Túlio Quintino
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2141 (2026).

The problem of deciding whether a set of quantum measurements is jointly measurable is known to be equivalent to determining whether a quantum assemblage is unsteerable. This problem can be formulated as a semidefinite program (SDP). However, the number of variables and constraints in such a formulation grows exponentially with the number of measurements, rendering it intractable for large measurement sets. In this work, we circumvent this problem by transforming the SDP into a hierarchy of linear programs that compute upper and lower bounds on the incompatibility robustness with a complexity that grows polynomially in the number of measurements. The hierarchy is guaranteed to converge and it can be applied to arbitrary measurements – including non-projective POVMs (Positive Operator-Valued Measures) – in arbitrary dimensions. While convergence becomes impractical in high dimensions, in the case of qubits our method reliably provides accurate upper and lower bounds for the incompatibility robustness of sets with several hundred measurements in a short time using a standard laptop. We also apply our methods to qutrits, obtaining non-trivial upper and lower bounds in scenarios that are otherwise intractable using the standard SDP approach, although such bounds are significantly looser than the ones obtained in the qubit case. Finally, we show how our methods can be used to construct local hidden state models for states (i.e., to prove that a state cannot lead to steering under any possible local measurements), or conversely, to certify that a given state exhibits steering; for two-qubit quantum states, our approach is comparable to, and in some cases outperforms, the current best methods.

.
tldr: This paper transforms the semidefinite program for joint measurability and steering into a hierarchy of linear programs, enabling efficient computation of incompatibility robustness for large measurement sets.
motivation: Determining whether a set of quantum measurements is jointly measurable or whether a state is steerable is computationally intractable for large measurement sets due to exponential growth of variables in the standard SDP formulation.
method: The authors reformulate the SDP as a hierarchy of linear programs that provide upper and lower bounds on incompatibility robustness, with polynomial complexity in the number of measurements. The hierarchy converges and applies to arbitrary POVMs in any dimension.
result: For qubits, the method reliably bounds incompatibility robustness for sets of hundreds of measurements on a standard laptop. For qutrits, non-trivial bounds are obtained in previously intractable scenarios. The method also constructs local hidden state models or certifies steering for two-qubit states, sometimes outperforming existing methods.
conclusion: The linear programming hierarchy offers a practical and scalable tool for analyzing measurement incompatibility and quantum steering, enabling studies of large measurement sets that were previously infeasible.

title: Tight Bounds For Quantum Phase Estimation And Related Problems
authors: Nikhil S. Mande And Ronald de Wolf
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2140 (2026).

Phase estimation, due to Kitaev [17], is one of the most fundamental subroutines in quantum computing. In the basic scenario, one is given black-box access to a unitary [MATH], and an eigenstate [MATH] of [MATH] with unknown eigenvalue [MATH], and the task is to estimate the eigenphase [MATH] within [MATH], with high probability. The cost of an algorithm for us is the number of applications of [MATH] and [MATH]. We tightly characterize the cost of several variants of phase estimation where we are no longer given an eigenstate, but are required to estimate the maximum eigenphase of [MATH], aided by advice in the form of states (or a unitary preparing those states) which are promised to have at least a certain overlap [MATH] with the top eigenspace. We give algorithms and nearly matching lower bounds for all ranges of parameters. We show that a small number of copies of the advice state (or of an advice-preparing unitary) are not significantly better than having no advice at all. We also show that having lots of advice (applications of the advice-preparing unitary) does not significantly reduce cost, and neither does knowledge of the eigenbasis of [MATH]. We immediately obtain a lower bound on the complexity of the Unitary recurrence time problem, resolving an open question of She and Yuen [29]. Lastly, we study how efficiently one can reduce the error probability in the basic phase-estimation scenario. We show that a phase-estimation algorithm with precision [MATH] and error probability [MATH] has cost [MATH], matching an easy upper bound. This contrasts with some other scenarios in quantum computing (e.g., search) where error-probability reduction costs only a factor [MATH]. Our lower bound uses a variant of the polynomial method with trigonometric polynomials.

.
tldr: This paper tightly characterizes the query complexity of quantum phase estimation with advice states, providing nearly matching upper and lower bounds for all parameter regimes.
motivation: Phase estimation is a fundamental subroutine in quantum computing, but its cost when given advice states (with overlap to the top eigenspace) was not well understood. The authors aim to close this gap and also resolve an open question about the Unitary recurrence time problem.
method: The authors develop algorithms for phase estimation with advice and prove nearly matching lower bounds using a variant of the polynomial method with trigonometric polynomials. They analyze the cost in terms of the number of applications of the unitary and its inverse, considering different amounts of advice.
result: They show that a small number of advice copies are not significantly better than no advice, and that having many advice applications does not significantly reduce cost. They also derive a tight bound for error probability reduction in basic phase estimation, showing cost scales as O(1/ε * log(1/δ)), matching an easy upper bound.
conclusion: The work provides a complete characterization of phase estimation with advice, resolving open questions and offering insights into the power of advice in quantum algorithms.

title: Qudit Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt Inequality And Nonlocality From Wigner Negativity
authors: Uta Isabella Meyer, Ivan Šupić, Damian Markham, And Frédéric Grosshans
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2139 (2026).

Nonlocality is an essential concept that distinguishes quantum from classical models and has been extensively studied in systems of qubits. For higher-dimensional systems, certain results for their two-level counterpart, like Bell violations with stabilizer states and Clifford operators, do not generalize. On the other hand, similar to continuous variable systems, Wigner negativity is necessary for nonlocality in qudit systems. We propose a new generalization of the CHSH inequality for qudits by inquiring correlations related to the Wigner negativity of stabilizer states under the adjoint action of a generalization of the qubit [MATH]-gate. A specified stabilizer state maximally violates the inequality among all qudit states based on its Wigner negativity. The Bell operator not only serves as a measure for the singlet fraction but also quantifies the volume of Wigner negativity. Additionally, we show how a bipartite entangled qudit state can serve as a witness for contextuality when it exhibits Wigner negativity. Furthermore, we identify rational-phase diagonal unitaries as the key resource that exactly reproduce the CGLMP and SATWAP violation with the maximally entangled state through simple phase-difference alignment.

.
tldr: Proposes a qudit CHSH inequality based on Wigner negativity, showing that stabilizer states with maximal Wigner negativity achieve maximal violation.
motivation: Generalizing Bell inequalities to higher-dimensional systems is challenging because known qubit results do not directly extend; this work aims to connect nonlocality to Wigner negativity in qudits.
method: Introduces a new CHSH-like inequality for qudits using correlations tied to Wigner negativity of stabilizer states under a generalized π/8 gate, and analyzes the Bell operator's relation to singlet fraction and Wigner negativity volume.
result: A specific stabilizer state maximally violates the inequality, and the Bell operator quantifies both singlet fraction and Wigner negativity; also shows that bipartite entangled qudit states with Wigner negativity witness contextuality.
conclusion: Wigner negativity is a necessary resource for nonlocality in qudit systems, and the proposed inequality provides a direct link between nonlocality and Wigner negativity, with implications for quantum information processing.

title: Distributing Graph States With A Photon-weaving Quantum Server
authors: Daniel Bhatti And Kenneth Goodenough
abstract: One of the key aims of quantum networks is the efficient distribution of multipartite entangled states among end users. While various architectures have been proposed, each comes with distinct advantages and limitations. Many designs depend on long-lived quantum memories and deterministic gates, which, while powerful, introduce considerable cost and technical challenges. Experimentally cheaper alternatives that circumvent these constraints are often limited to specific types of entanglement and a specific number of users. Here, we present an experiment-friendly quantum server that relies only on linear optical elements, offering a flexible approach to multipartite entanglement distribution. Our so-called photon-weaving quantum server can generate and distribute one of several locally nonequivalent graph states, including Greenberger–Horne–Zeilinger (GHZ) states, as well as path, cycle, and caterpillar graph states. This is achieved through two distinct fusion protocols, i.e. multiphoton graph-state fusion (graph-state weaving) and multiphoton GHZ-state fusion (GHZ-state weaving), and can readily be implemented.
tldr: Proposes an experiment-friendly quantum server using linear optics to distribute various graph states, including GHZ states, via two fusion protocols.
motivation: Efficient distribution of multipartite entangled states is key for quantum networks, but existing architectures often require costly long-lived quantum memories and deterministic gates.
method: The photon-weaving quantum server uses only linear optical elements and implements two fusion protocols: graph-state weaving and GHZ-state weaving to generate and distribute graph states.
result: The server can generate and distribute several locally nonequivalent graph states, including GHZ, path, cycle, and caterpillar graph states, using the two fusion protocols.
conclusion: This approach offers a flexible, experiment-friendly alternative for multipartite entanglement distribution in quantum networks, avoiding the need for quantum memories and deterministic gates.

title: Phase-controlled Thermal Amplification In A Quantum Thermal Transistor
authors: Xiaoyun Wang And Dazhi Xu
abstract: We investigate phase-controlled heat transport in a quantum thermal transistor composed of three coupled two-level systems, each connected to an independent thermal reservoir. Using a nonsecular Redfield master equation, we show that a gauge-invariant phase in the triangular coupling loop provides an efficient control knob beyond reservoir temperatures: at fixed temperature bias, tuning the phase strongly modulates the steady-state heat currents and can generate pronounced thermal amplification, whereby a small variation of the control current induces large changes in the currents at the other two terminals. We further analyze how the amplification depends on the reservoir temperature as well as on the intersystem couplings, identifying regimes of enhanced performance. To clarify the underlying mechanism, we develop a complementary weak-coupling theory based on a local Lindblad equation and second-order cumulant expansion. This analysis shows that the phase first enters the exchange coherences and is then transferred to the populations through loop interference, while the heat currents are dominated by the resulting population corrections. Our results establish phase engineering as a flexible route to regulating heat flow and thermal amplification in multi-terminal quantum thermal devices.
tldr: This paper demonstrates phase-controlled heat transport and thermal amplification in a quantum thermal transistor using a nonsecular Redfield master equation.
motivation: To explore phase engineering as a control knob for heat flow in multi-terminal quantum thermal devices, beyond temperature bias.
method: A nonsecular Redfield master equation is used to model three coupled two-level systems connected to independent reservoirs, with a gauge-invariant phase in the triangular coupling loop.
result: Tuning the phase strongly modulates steady-state heat currents and generates pronounced thermal amplification, with performance depending on reservoir temperatures and intersystem couplings.
conclusion: Phase engineering provides a flexible route to regulate heat flow and thermal amplification in quantum thermal devices, advancing quantum thermodynamics.

title: Gap Between Quantum Theory Based On Real And Complex Numbers Is Arbitrarily Large
authors: Shubhayan Sarkar, David Trillo, Marc Olivier Renou And Remigiusz Augusiak
abstract: Quantum information theory, the formalism for representing information contained in quantum systems, is based on complex Hilbert spaces. It was recently shown that in quantum networks involving three parties with nontrivial locality constraints, this formalism predicts correlations that cannot be explained by real quantum theory, a variant of quantum mechanics based on real Hilbert spaces. In this work, we study a scenario with parties sharing quantum systems in a star network. We then construct a multipartite Bell inequality that exhibits a gap between quantum theory and its variant based on real numbers, which grows linearly with , and is thus arbitrarily large in the asymptotic limit. This implies, that, as the number of parties grows, Hilbert space formalism based on real numbers becomes exceedingly worse at describing complex networks of quantum systems. We also compute the tolerance of this gap to experimental errors.
tldr: This paper shows that the gap between real and complex quantum theory in star networks grows linearly with the number of parties, making real quantum theory arbitrarily worse.
motivation: Recent work demonstrated that complex Hilbert spaces are necessary to describe certain quantum correlations in networks. This paper aims to quantify how much worse real quantum theory becomes as network size increases.
method: The authors construct a multipartite Bell inequality for a star network and analyze the violation achievable by complex versus real quantum theory, deriving a linear lower bound on the gap.
result: The gap between complex and real quantum correlations grows linearly with the number of parties, becoming arbitrarily large in the asymptotic limit. The tolerance to experimental errors is also computed.
conclusion: Real quantum theory is fundamentally limited in describing large quantum networks, highlighting the necessity of complex Hilbert spaces for quantum information.

title: Fast Quantum Measurement Tomography With Optimal Error Bounds
authors: Leonardo Zambrano, Sergi Ramos-Calderer, And Richard Kueng
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2162 (2026).

We present a two-step protocol for quantum measurement tomography that is light on classical co-processing cost and still achieves optimal sample complexity. Given measurement data from a known probe state ensemble, we first apply least-squares estimation to produce an unconstrained approximation of the POVM, and then project this estimate onto the set of valid quantum measurements. For a POVM with [MATH] outcomes acting on a [MATH]-dimensional system, we show that the protocol requires [MATH] samples to achieve error [MATH] in worst-case distance, and [MATH] samples in average-case distance. We further establish two matching sample complexity lower bounds of [MATH] and [MATH] for any non-adaptive, single-copy POVM tomography protocol. Hence, our projected least squares POVM tomography is sample-optimal in both the dimension and the number of outcomes for both distances. Our method admits an analytic form when using global or local 2-designs as probe ensembles and enables rigorous non-asymptotic error guarantees. Finally, we also complement our findings with empirical performance studies carried out on a noisy superconducting quantum computer with flux-tunable transmon qubits.

.
tldr: A sample-optimal quantum measurement tomography protocol using projected least squares estimation with rigorous error bounds.
motivation: Existing quantum measurement tomography protocols are either computationally expensive or lack optimal sample complexity, hindering practical characterization of quantum devices.
method: The protocol first applies least-squares estimation to measurement data from known probe states, then projects the estimate onto the set of valid POVMs. It uses global or local 2-designs as probe ensembles.
result: The protocol achieves optimal sample complexity in both worst-case and average-case distance, with matching lower bounds. It is demonstrated on a noisy superconducting quantum computer.
conclusion: The proposed method is sample-optimal, computationally light, and provides rigorous non-asymptotic error guarantees, making it practical for quantum device characterization.

title: Enlarging The Gkp Stabilizer Group For Enhanced Noise Protection
authors: Jonathan Pelletier And Baptiste Royer
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2156 (2026).

Encoding a qubit in a larger Hilbert space of an oscillator is an efficient way to protect its quantum information against decoherence. Promising examples of such bosonic encodings are the Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) codes. In this work, we investigate how redefining the stabilizer group of the GKP codes to include all operations with trivial action on the code space can contribute to the search for an optimal implementation of a logical circuit when it is affected by noise. We find the generators of the Gaussian stabilizer group, allowing us to search for different physical implementations of a Clifford operation. We then propose an algorithm that finds the optimal implementation of a given logical Clifford circuit on GKP codes, such that the state is less affected by loss errors during the computation. Finally, we demonstrate numerically, with logical randomized benchmarking, that such a compiler can increase the lifetime of square-GKP qubits while running Clifford circuits, compared to a random walk compiler.

.
tldr: This paper enlarges the GKP stabilizer group to include all operations with trivial action on the code space, enabling optimal implementation of logical Clifford circuits with enhanced noise protection.
motivation: GKP codes are promising for protecting quantum information in oscillators, but finding optimal physical implementations of logical circuits under noise is challenging.
method: The authors find generators of the Gaussian stabilizer group and propose an algorithm that searches for the optimal implementation of a given logical Clifford circuit on GKP codes to minimize loss errors.
result: Numerical simulations using logical randomized benchmarking show that the compiler increases the lifetime of square-GKP qubits during Clifford circuits compared to a random walk compiler.
conclusion: Redefining the stabilizer group and optimizing circuit implementations can significantly improve noise protection for GKP codes.

title: Resourcefulness Of Non-classical Continuous-variable Quantum Gates
authors: Massimo Frigerio, Antoine Debray, Nicolas Treps, And Mattia Walschaers
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2155 (2026).

In continuous-variable quantum computation, identifying key elements that enable a quantum computational advantage is a long-standing issue. Starting from the standard results on the necessity of Wigner negativity, we develop a comprehensive and versatile approach in which the techniques of [MATH]-ordered quasiprobabilities are exploited to provide rigorous statements on the simulability of photonic quantum circuits consisting of previously characterized gates and thereby identifying the contribution of each quantum gate to the potential achievement of quantum computational advantage. This is achieved by means of an analysis of the so-called transfer function, allowing us to highlight the resourcefulness of a gate set. As such this technique can be straightforwardly applied to current continuous-variables quantum circuits, while also constraining the tolerable amount of losses above which any potential quantum advantage can be ruled out. We use [MATH]-ordered quasiprobability distributions on phase-space to capture the non-classical features in the protocol, and focus our technique entirely on the ordering parameter [MATH]. This allows us to highlight the resourcefulness and robustness to loss of a universal set of unitary gates comprising three distinct Gaussian gates and any non-Gaussian unitary gate, providing important insight on the role of non-Gaussianity.

.
tldr: This paper develops a framework using s-ordered quasiprobabilities to quantify the non-classical resources of continuous-variable quantum gates, linking Wigner negativity to quantum computational advantage.
motivation: Identifying which quantum gates provide a computational advantage in continuous-variable quantum computation is a long-standing issue; the authors aim to develop a rigorous method to assess the resourcefulness of gate sets.
method: The authors exploit s-ordered quasiprobability distributions on phase space and analyze the transfer function of quantum circuits to characterize the non-classical features of Gaussian and non-Gaussian unitary gates.
result: They provide a comprehensive approach to determine the simulability of photonic quantum circuits and identify the contribution of each gate to quantum advantage, including constraints on tolerable losses.
conclusion: The technique offers a versatile tool for assessing the resourcefulness of continuous-variable quantum gates and can be applied to current quantum circuits, highlighting the role of non-Gaussianity.

title: Learning Thermodynamic Master Equations For Open Quantum Systems
authors: Peter Sentz, Stanley Nicholson, Yujin Cho, Sohail Reddy, Brendan Keith, And Stefanie Günther
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2151 (2026).

The characterization of Hamiltonians and other components of open quantum dynamical systems plays a crucial role in quantum computing and other applications. Scientific machine learning techniques have been applied to this problem in a variety of ways, including by modeling with deep neural networks. However, the majority of mathematical models describing open quantum systems are linear, and the natural nonlinearities in learnable models have not been incorporated using physical principles. We present a data-driven model for open quantum systems that includes learnable, thermodynamically consistent terms. The trained model is interpretable, as it directly estimates the system Hamiltonian and linear components of coupling to the environment. We validate the model on synthetic two and three-level data, as well as experimental two-level data collected from a quantum device at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory.

.
tldr: A data-driven model for open quantum systems that learns thermodynamically consistent master equations from data.
motivation: Characterizing Hamiltonians and environmental couplings in open quantum systems is crucial for quantum computing, but existing models often lack thermodynamic consistency.
method: The authors propose a neural network model that incorporates learnable, thermodynamically consistent terms, directly estimating the system Hamiltonian and linear coupling components.
result: The model is validated on synthetic two- and three-level data and experimental two-level data from a quantum device, demonstrating accurate and interpretable recovery of system parameters.
conclusion: The approach provides a physically principled, interpretable machine learning framework for modeling open quantum systems, with potential applications in quantum device characterization and control.

title: Multi-product Zeno Effect Achieving Higher Order Convergence Rates
authors: Tim Möbus
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2148 (2026).

The quantum Zeno effect is a fundamental mechanism for implementing the effective dynamics of projected Hamiltonian and Lindbladian systems. It approximates the target projected evolution by interleaving Hamiltonian or Lindblad dynamics with quantum operations associated with the desired subspace. In contrast to the related Trotter product formula, the best-known convergence rate of the quantum Zeno effect is typically limited to order [MATH]. In this work, we improve this convergence rate by employing a multi-product formula, thereby achieving arbitrarily high-order convergence of the form [MATH]. This yields an improved approximation scheme for Zeno-like expectation values via an efficient post-processing method. The approach combines a modified Chernoff lemma, an adapted Dunford-Segal approximation, holomorphic functional calculus, and Chebyshev interpolation. We illustrate the method with the bosonic cat code and also consider the broader class of systems governed by the Bang-Bang decoupling method.

.
tldr: This paper improves the convergence rate of the quantum Zeno effect to arbitrarily high order using multi-product formulas, with applications to projected dynamics and bang-bang decoupling.
motivation: The quantum Zeno effect typically has limited convergence rate; achieving higher-order convergence can improve approximations of projected Hamiltonian and Lindbladian dynamics.
method: The authors combine a modified Chernoff lemma, Dunford-Segal approximation, holomorphic functional calculus, and Chebyshev interpolation to construct a multi-product formula that yields higher-order convergence.
result: They demonstrate arbitrarily high-order convergence rates for the quantum Zeno effect and illustrate the method with the bosonic cat code and bang-bang decoupling.
conclusion: The multi-product Zeno effect provides a more efficient approximation scheme for Zeno-like expectation values, with potential applications in quantum control and simulation.

title: On The Addressability Problem On Css Codes
authors: Jérôme Guyot And Samuel Jaques
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2145 (2026).

Recent discoveries in asymptotically good quantum codes have intensified research on their application in quantum computation and fault-tolerant operations. This study focuses on the addressability problem within CSS codes: we ask what circuits might implement logical gates on strict subsets of logical qubits. With some notion of fault-tolerance, we prove several impossibility results: for CSS codes with non-zero rate, one cannot address a logical [MATH], [MATH], [MATH], or [MATH] to any non-empty strict subset of logical qubits using a circuit made only from 1-local Clifford gates. Furthermore, we show that one cannot permute the logical qubits in a code purely by permuting the physical qubits, if the rate of the code is (asymptotically) greater than 1/3 and the distance is at least 3. We can show a similar no-go result for [MATH]s and [MATH]s between two such high-rate codes, albeit under a more restrictive assumption on the circuit, which we call "global" (though recent addressable CCZ gates use global circuits). This work pioneers the study of distance-preserving addressability in quantum codes, mainly by considering automorphisms of the code. This perspective offers new insights and potential directions for future research. We argue that studying this trade off between addressability and efficiency of the codes is essential to understand better how to do efficient quantum computation.

.
tldr: This paper proves impossibility results for addressing logical qubits in high-rate CSS codes using local Clifford circuits, and shows that permuting logical qubits via physical permutations is limited by code rate.
motivation: Asymptotically good quantum codes promise efficient fault-tolerant computation, but it is unclear how to perform logical operations on subsets of logical qubits without affecting others. Understanding addressability is crucial for designing practical quantum circuits.
method: The authors use automorphism theory of CSS codes and combinatorial arguments to derive no-go theorems for implementing logical gates on strict subsets of logical qubits with 1-local Clifford circuits, and for permuting logical qubits via physical permutations.
result: For CSS codes with non-zero rate, one cannot address logical X, Z, H, or S gates to any non-empty strict subset of logical qubits using 1-local Clifford circuits. Also, permuting logical qubits by physical permutations is impossible if the code rate > 1/3 and distance ≥ 3.
conclusion: There is a fundamental trade-off between addressability and code efficiency in CSS codes, which must be considered for designing fault-tolerant quantum computers.

title: Active Quantum Reservoir Engineering: Using A Qubit To Manipulate Its Environment
authors: Marcelo Janovitch, Matteo Brunelli, And Patrick P. Potts
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2143 (2026).

Quantum reservoir engineering leverages dissipative processes to achieve desired behaviour, with applications ranging from entanglement generation to quantum error correction. Therein, a structured environment acts as an entropy sink for the system and no time-dependent control over the system is required. We develop a theoretical framework for active reservoir engineering, where time-dependent control over a quantum system is used to manipulate its environment. In this case, the system may act as an entropy sink for the environment. Our framework captures the dynamical interplay between system and environment, and provides an intuitive picture of how finite-size effects and system-environment correlations allow for manipulating the environment by repeated initialisation of the quantum system. We illustrate our results with two examples: a superconducting qubit coupled to an environment of two-level systems and a semiconducting quantum dot coupled to nuclear spins. In both scenarios, we find qualitative agreement with previous experimental results, illustrating how active control can unlock new functionalities in open quantum systems.

.
tldr: A theoretical framework for active reservoir engineering where time-dependent control over a quantum system manipulates its environment, enabling the system to act as an entropy sink.
motivation: Standard quantum reservoir engineering uses structured environments as entropy sinks without active control; this work explores the reverse scenario where active control on the system can manipulate the environment, unlocking new functionalities.
method: The authors develop a theoretical framework capturing the dynamical interplay between system and environment, including finite-size effects and correlations, and illustrate it with two examples: a superconducting qubit coupled to two-level systems and a quantum dot coupled to nuclear spins.
result: The framework provides an intuitive picture of how repeated initialization of the quantum system can manipulate the environment, and qualitative agreement with previous experimental results is found.
conclusion: Active control can unlock new functionalities in open quantum systems, with potential applications in quantum thermodynamics and information processing.

title: Heralded Ultrafast Generation Of Macroscopic Quantum States In Matter With Bright Squeezed Vacuum Light
authors: Shohei Imai
abstract: We show that bright squeezed vacuum light, combined with a single-shot quadrature measurement of the post-interaction light, enables the ultrafast generation of macroscopic quantum states in matter. Although in the weak-coupling regime multiphoton quantum light leaves the unconditional matter state as a classical mixture due to light–matter entanglement, quadrature-based heralding prepares the matter in a Gaussian-weighted quantum superposition of laser-driven matter states. For an ensemble of resonantly electric-dipole-coupled two-level systems, this heralding dynamics acts as a Gaussian filter with respect to the electric polarization, with brighter squeezed-vacuum light accelerating the preparation of the zero-eigenvalue Dicke state. Counter-rotating terms further drive a stroboscopic transition from this Dicke state to a cat-like state. Our results open a route to ultrafast engineering of macroscopic quantum matter with strong-field quantum light.
tldr: Bright squeezed vacuum light combined with quadrature measurement enables ultrafast generation of macroscopic quantum states in matter.
motivation: To achieve ultrafast preparation of macroscopic quantum states in matter using bright squeezed vacuum light, overcoming the limitation of weak-coupling regime where unconditional states become classical mixtures.
method: The authors propose a heralding scheme based on single-shot quadrature measurement of post-interaction bright squeezed vacuum light, which acts as a Gaussian filter on the matter state, preparing Gaussian-weighted superpositions of laser-driven states.
result: For an ensemble of two-level systems, the heralding prepares the zero-eigenvalue Dicke state, and counter-rotating terms drive a stroboscopic transition to a cat-like state, with brighter light accelerating the process.
conclusion: This work opens a route to ultrafast engineering of macroscopic quantum matter using strong-field quantum light, relevant for hybrid quantum systems combining light and matter.

title: Optimal Schedule Of Multi-channel Quantum Zeno Dragging With Application To Solving The k-SAT Problem
authors: Yipei Zhang, Alain Sarlette, Philippe Lewalle, Tathagata Karmakar, Thilo Scharnhorst, And K. Birgitta Whaley
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2167 (2026).

Quantum Zeno dragging enables the preparation of common eigenstates of a set of observables by frequent measurement and adiabatic-like modulation of the measurement basis. In this work, we present a deeper analysis of multi-channel Zeno dragging using generalized measurements, i.e. simultaneously measuring a set of non-commuting observables that vary slowly in time, to drag the state towards a target subspace. For concreteness, we will focus on a measurement-driven approach to solving k-SAT problems as examples. We first compute some analytical upper bounds on the convergence time, including the effect of finite measurement time resolution. We then apply optimal control theory to obtain the optimal dragging schedule that lower bounds the convergence time, for low-dimensional settings. This study provides a theoretical foundation for multi-channel Zeno dragging and its optimization, and also serves as a guide for designing optimal dragging schedules for quantum information tasks including measurement-driven quantum algorithms.

.
tldr: This paper analyzes multi-channel quantum Zeno dragging with generalized measurements and applies optimal control to schedule measurements for solving k-SAT problems.
motivation: Quantum Zeno dragging can prepare common eigenstates of observables, which is useful for measurement-driven quantum algorithms like solving k-SAT.
method: The authors compute analytical upper bounds on convergence time, including finite measurement resolution effects, and apply optimal control theory to find the optimal dragging schedule in low-dimensional settings.
result: They derive lower bounds on convergence time and demonstrate optimal schedules that minimize the time to reach the target subspace.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical foundation for multi-channel Zeno dragging and offers guidance for designing optimal schedules in quantum information tasks.

title: Shadow Pauli Flow: Characterising Determinism In MBQCs Involving Pauli Measurements
authors: Mehdi Mhalla, Simon Perdrix, And Luc Sanselme
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2163 (2026).

We introduce a new characterisation of determinism in Measurement-Based Quantum Computing (MBQC). The one-way model consists in performing local measurements over a large entangled state represented by a graph. The ability to perform an overall deterministic computation requires a correction strategy because of the non-determinism of each measurement. The existence of such a correction strategy depends on the underlying open graph, which is a description of the resource state together with the basis of the performed measurements. GFlow is a well-known graphical characterisation of robust determinism in MBQC when every measurement is performed in some specific planes of the Bloch sphere. While Pauli measurements are ubiquitous in MBQC, GFlow fails to be necessary for determinism when a measurement-based quantum computation involves Pauli measurements. Pauli Flow was designed as a generalisation of GFlow to handle MBQC with Pauli measurements, and guarantees robust determinism, however, it has been shown more recently that it fails to be a necessary condition. Our contribution is twofold. First, we demonstrate that Pauli flow is actually necessary for robust determinism in a weaker sense: given an open graph, i.e. a resource state, a deterministic computation can be driven iff it has a Pauli flow. However, the Pauli flows do not reflect all the possible correction strategies over a particular resource state, and properties like measurement order or computational depth are not necessarily reflected by a Pauli flow. Thus, to characterise determinism in full generality, we introduce a further extension called Shadow Pauli Flow that we prove necessary and sufficient for robust determinism: An MBQC is robustly deterministic if and only if its correction strategy is consistent with a Shadow Pauli flow. Furthermore, we show that Shadow Pauli flow can be computed in polynomial time.

.
tldr: Introduces Shadow Pauli Flow, a necessary and sufficient condition for robust determinism in measurement-based quantum computing with Pauli measurements.
motivation: Previous characterizations like GFlow and Pauli Flow were insufficient for MBQC involving Pauli measurements; a complete characterization was needed.
method: Extends the concept of Pauli Flow to Shadow Pauli Flow, proving its necessity and sufficiency for robust determinism, and provides a polynomial-time algorithm to compute it.
result: Shadow Pauli Flow is both necessary and sufficient for robust determinism in MBQC with Pauli measurements, and can be computed efficiently.
conclusion: This work provides a complete graphical characterization of determinism in MBQC with Pauli measurements, enabling better understanding and design of deterministic measurement-based computations.

title: Exploring Imaginary Coordinates: Disparity In The Shape Of Quantum State Space In Even And Odd Dimensions
authors: Simon Morelli, Santiago Llorens, And Jens Siewert
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2153 (2026).

The state of a finite-dimensional quantum system is described by a density matrix that can be decomposed into a real diagonal, a real off-diagonal and and an imaginary off-diagonal part. The latter plays a peculiar role. While it is intuitively clear that some of the imaginary coordinates cannot have the same extension as their real counterparts the precise relation is not obvious. We give a complete characterization of the constraints in terms of tight inequalities for real and imaginary Bloch-type coordinates. Our description entails a three-dimensional Bloch ball-type model for the state space. We uncover a surprising qualitative difference for the state-space boundaries in even and odd dimensions.

.
tldr: This paper fully characterizes the constraints on imaginary Bloch coordinates for finite-dimensional quantum states, revealing a parity-dependent shape of the state space.
motivation: Understanding the geometry of quantum state space is fundamental to quantum information theory, and the role of imaginary coordinates was not fully characterized.
method: The authors derive tight inequalities for real and imaginary Bloch-type coordinates, constructing a three-dimensional Bloch ball model for the state space.
result: They find a surprising qualitative difference in the state-space boundaries between even and odd dimensions.
conclusion: The work provides a complete characterization of imaginary coordinate constraints, deepening our understanding of quantum state space geometry.

title: Query And Depth Upper Bounds For Quantum Unitaries Via Grover Search
authors: Gregory Rosenthal
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2144 (2026).

We prove that any [MATH]-qubit unitary can be implemented (i) approximately in time [MATH] with query access to an appropriate classical oracle, and also (ii) exactly by a circuit of depth [MATH] with one- and two-qubit gates and [MATH] ancillae. The proofs involve similar reductions to Grover search. The proof of (ii) also involves a linear-depth construction of arbitrary quantum states using one- and two-qubit gates (in fact, this can be improved to constant depth with the addition of fanout and generalized Toffoli gates) which may be of independent interest. We also prove a matching [MATH] lower bound for (i) and (ii) for a certain class of implementations.

.
tldr: This paper proves upper bounds on query complexity and circuit depth for implementing arbitrary quantum unitaries using Grover search, with matching lower bounds for certain implementations.
motivation: Understanding the minimal resources (queries, depth) needed to implement arbitrary quantum operations is fundamental to quantum computing and information theory.
method: The authors reduce unitary implementation to Grover search, constructing circuits that approximate or exactly realize any unitary with given query and depth bounds, and prove lower bounds via adversary methods.
result: Any n-qubit unitary can be implemented approximately in O(2^{n/2}) time with query access to a classical oracle, and exactly by a circuit of depth O(2^{n/2}) with one- and two-qubit gates and O(2^{n/2}) ancillae. A matching Ω(2^{n/2}) lower bound is shown for a class of implementations.
conclusion: Grover search provides a general method for implementing arbitrary unitaries with exponential savings in query and depth compared to naive approaches, though the bounds are still exponential in the number of qubits.

title: Non-Markovian Quantum Mpemba Effect In Strongly Correlated Quantum Dots
authors: Yuandong Wang And Jianhua Wei
abstract: Harnessing non-Markovian effects has emerged as a resource for quantum control, where a structured environment can act as a quantum memory. We investigate the quench dynamics from specific initial states to equilibrium steady states in strongly correlated quantum dot systems. The distance between quantum states is quantified using the Bures metric, which endows the space of reduced density matrices with a Riemannian geometric structure. Using the numerically exact hierarchical equations of motion method, we demonstrate a quantum Mpemba effect (QME) arising from non-Markovianity. Unlike previous studies centered on non-interacting limits, we reveal a distinct non-Markovian QME uniquely driven by the initial-state-dependent formation of the many-body Kondo resonance. Furthermore, by tracking the dynamical evolution in the generalized Bloch parameter space, we uncover an intrinsic QME. This trajectory-dependent analysis provides a rigorous geometric perspective on the circuitous relaxation pathways driven by Kondo correlations. Our results underscore the critical role of memory effects in quantum quench dynamics and suggest new pathways for controlling anomalous relaxation in open quantum systems.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a non-Markovian quantum Mpemba effect in strongly correlated quantum dots, driven by Kondo correlations and memory effects.
motivation: Understanding anomalous relaxation in open quantum systems is important for quantum control; the quantum Mpemba effect offers a way to harness non-Markovianity.
method: The authors use the numerically exact hierarchical equations of motion method to simulate quench dynamics and quantify state distance via the Bures metric.
result: They reveal a distinct non-Markovian QME uniquely driven by initial-state-dependent formation of the many-body Kondo resonance, and uncover an intrinsic QME in generalized Bloch parameter space.
conclusion: Memory effects play a critical role in quantum quench dynamics, and the results suggest new pathways for controlling anomalous relaxation in open quantum systems.

title: Saturation Attack Of The Microwave-propagated Continuous Variable Quantum Key Distribution In Open Air
authors: Wenqi Peng, Xuan Li, Yongxin Feng, Xiu-Bo Chen And Ying Guo
abstract: Continuous variable quantum key distribution (CVQKD) can achieve the secure communication between two distant legitimate users. The microwave CVQKD exhibits stronger robustness than the optical CVQKD in transmitting quantum signals and accordingly has broad application prospects in quantum networks. Although the microwave CVQKD does not rely on the traditional optical fibers to transmit quantum signals, its practical security is still vulnerable to saturation attacks. In view of this security vulnerability, we generalize saturation attacks to microwave CVQKD and clarify the impact of saturation attacks on the parameter estimation of microwave systems. Two saturation attack schemes are further compared, one based on displacement control alone and the other on joint displacement and gain control. To mitigate the negative impacts caused by this attack, we propose a countermeasure based on the quantum nearest neighbor algorithm, which can detect saturation attacks by measuring unknown quantum states. In addition, the influence of microwave antennas on the security of the communication system is assessed, confirming that antenna gain plays a key role in determining both the secret key rate and the maximum transmission distance.
tldr: This paper generalizes saturation attacks to microwave continuous-variable QKD and proposes a countermeasure using quantum nearest neighbor algorithm.
motivation: Microwave CVQKD offers robustness for quantum networks but is vulnerable to saturation attacks; the paper aims to analyze and mitigate this threat.
method: The authors model two saturation attack schemes (displacement control alone vs. joint displacement and gain control) and propose a detection method based on quantum nearest neighbor algorithm.
result: The analysis shows that antenna gain significantly affects secret key rate and maximum transmission distance; the proposed countermeasure can detect saturation attacks.
conclusion: Saturation attacks pose a practical security risk to microwave CVQKD, but can be mitigated by the proposed detection method, enhancing the security of quantum networks.

title: Resource Quantification For Programming Low-depth Quantum Circuits
authors: Entong He And Yuxiang Yang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2166 (2026).

Noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices pave the way for implementing quantum algorithms that offer quantum advantages over their classical counterparts. Due to the intrinsic noise and decoherence in the physical system, NISQ machines are naturally modeled as large-scale, low-depth quantum circuits. In practice, executing such circuits requires sending program states that encode the relevant instructions to a programmable quantum computer, typically through a cloud service. Existing programming approaches designed for generic unitary transformations are computationally inefficient in the low-depth setting, and therefore remain unsatisfactory. As such, to realize NISQ algorithms, it is crucial to find an efficient way to program low-depth circuits as the number of qubits [MATH] increases. Here, we investigate the circuit complexity and the size of quantum memory, known as the program cost, required to program low-depth brickwork circuits. We establish a tight worst-case program cost of [MATH] for universally programming low-depth brickwork circuits in the large-[MATH] regime. Moreover, we analyze the trade-off between the cost of describing the layout of local gates and the cost of programming them to implement the target unitaries via the light-cone argument. Our findings suggest that faithful gate-wise programming is essentially optimal in the low-depth regime.

.
tldr: This paper establishes tight worst-case program cost for programming low-depth brickwork circuits, showing that faithful gate-wise programming is essentially optimal.
motivation: Existing programming approaches for generic unitary transformations are inefficient for low-depth circuits, which are crucial for NISQ devices. An efficient method to program such circuits is needed as qubit count increases.
method: The authors analyze circuit complexity and quantum memory size (program cost) required to program low-depth brickwork circuits, using a light-cone argument to study the trade-off between describing local gate layouts and programming them.
result: They establish a tight worst-case program cost for universally programming low-depth brickwork circuits in the large-qubit regime, and show that faithful gate-wise programming is essentially optimal.
conclusion: The findings provide a resource quantification for programming low-depth circuits, which is important for NISQ algorithm implementation.

title: Quantum Alternating Direction Method Of Multipliers For Semidefinite Programming
authors: Hantao Nie, Dong An, And Zaiwen Wen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2154 (2026).

Semidefinite programming (SDP) is a fundamental convex optimization problem with wide-ranging applications. However, solving large-scale instances remains computationally challenging due to the high cost of solving linear systems and performing eigenvalue decompositions. In this paper, we present a quantum alternating direction method of multipliers (QADMM) for SDPs, building on recent advances in quantum computing. An inexact ADMM framework is developed, which tolerates errors in the iterates arising from block-encoding approximation and quantum measurement. Within this robust scheme, we design a polynomial proximal operator to address the semidefinite conic constraints and apply the quantum singular value transformation to accelerate the most costly projection updates. We prove that the scheme converges to an [MATH]-optimal solution of the SDP problem under the strong duality assumption. A detailed complexity analysis shows that the QADMM algorithm achieves favorable scaling with respect to dimension compared to the classical ADMM algorithm and quantum interior point methods, highlighting its potential for solving large-scale SDPs.

.
tldr: A quantum algorithm for semidefinite programming using ADMM and quantum singular value transformation, achieving better dimension scaling than classical methods.
motivation: Semidefinite programming is fundamental but computationally expensive for large instances; quantum computing may offer speedups.
method: Develops an inexact ADMM framework tolerant to errors from block-encoding and measurement, and uses quantum singular value transformation for projection updates.
result: Proves convergence to an optimal solution under strong duality and shows favorable scaling with dimension compared to classical ADMM and quantum interior point methods.
conclusion: QADMM is a promising quantum algorithm for large-scale SDPs, though practical implementation remains challenging.
keywords: quantum alternating direction method of multipliers

title: Steady-state Entanglement Harvesting For Two Rotating Atoms In A Cylindrical Cavity
authors: Hong-Tao Zheng, Xiang-Fa Zhou, Guang-Can Guo And Zheng-Wei Zhou
abstract: We study the entanglement dynamics of two rotating atoms (with two internal levels and ) in a cylindrical cavity, which interact with a massless scalar field in vacuum satisfying the Dirichlet boundary condition. Our analysis demonstrates that it is possible to obtain the steady-state entanglement under two types of resonant conditions. For two identical atoms with the same world-line, the system reduces to the usual dissipative Dicke model at the first resonant condition where and are the energy splitting and the angular velocity of the th atom, and is the Lorentz factor. The entangled steady-state takes the form where and are constant, which is consistent with the previous study (see 2022 Phys. Rev. D 106 105028). For two atoms with different world-lines, the system suffers from a significant mixed joint dissipation process at the second resonant condition , and reaches an entangled steady-state as . Moreover, with the help of the cavity, we can obtain a much higher concurrence in the final states by changing the relative ratio of the two orbital radii. Our work thus provides a more effective way for the extraction of steady-state entanglement from the vacuum via the analogue Unruh effect for two rotating atoms in a cylindrical cavity.
tldr: Two rotating atoms in a cylindrical cavity can harvest steady-state entanglement from the vacuum via the analogue Unruh effect, with higher concurrence achievable by tuning orbital radii.
motivation: To study entanglement harvesting from vacuum in a rotating frame, which is relevant to understanding quantum information in non-inertial settings and the Unruh effect.
method: The authors model two two-level atoms rotating in a cylindrical cavity with Dirichlet boundary conditions, interacting with a massless scalar field. They derive master equations and analyze resonant conditions for steady-state entanglement.
result: Steady-state entanglement is achieved under two resonant conditions, with the second condition involving mixed joint dissipation. The cavity allows higher concurrence by adjusting the ratio of orbital radii.
conclusion: The work provides an effective method for extracting steady-state entanglement from vacuum using rotating atoms in a cavity, relevant to quantum information in accelerated frames.

title: Invariant Nonequilibrium Dynamics In Gene Regulation Optimize Information Flow
authors: Benjamin Zolleralexis Bénichouthomas Gregorgašper Tkačikahttps://ror.org/0495fxg12department Of Stem Cell And Developmental Biology, CNRS UMR3738 Paris Cité, Institut Pasteur, Paris Fr-75015, Francebhttps://ror.org/03gnh5541institute Of Science And Technology Austria, Klosterneuburg At-3400, Austriachttps://ror.org/00hx57361joseph Henry Laboratories Of Physics, Lewis-Sigler Institute For Integrative Genomics, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544
abstract:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Volume 123, Issue 28, July 2026.
SignificanceEukaryotic genes switch on and off stochastically, yet cells regulate gene expression with remarkable precision by biasing the probability of switching. Recent experiments revealed a surprising and unexplained constraint: The characteristic ...
tldr: This paper studies stochastic gene regulation dynamics and shows that invariant nonequilibrium dynamics optimize information flow between input and output.
motivation: Recent experiments revealed a surprising constraint on gene switching rates; the authors aim to explain this constraint using information-theoretic and thermodynamic principles.
method: They model gene regulation as a nonequilibrium stochastic process and analyze the information-theoretic capacity of the system under constraints on switching rates.
result: They find that the experimentally observed constraint corresponds to an optimal trade-off between speed and accuracy, maximizing mutual information between regulatory signals and gene expression.
conclusion: Invariant nonequilibrium dynamics in gene regulation are a signature of optimal information flow, linking thermodynamics and information theory in a biological context.

title: Exact Quantum Many-Body Scars In 2d Quantum Gauge Models
authors: Yuan Miao, Linhao Li, Hosho Katsura, And Masahito Yamazaki
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2164 (2026).

Quantum many-body scars (QMBS) serve as important examples of ergodicity-breaking phenomena in quantum many-body systems. Despite recent extensive studies, exact QMBS are rare in dimensions higher than one. In this paper, we study a two-dimensional quantum [MATH] gauge model that is dual to a two-dimensional spin-[MATH] XY model defined on bipartite graphs. We identify the exact eigenstates of the XY model with a tower structure as exact QMBS. Exploiting the duality transformation, we show that the exact QMBS of the XY model (and XXZ model) after the transformation are the exact QMBS of the dual [MATH] gauge model. This construction is versatile and has potential applications for finding new QMBS in other higher-dimensional models.

.
tldr: This paper constructs exact quantum many-body scars in a 2D quantum gauge model via duality to an XY model.
motivation: Quantum many-body scars are rare in higher dimensions; the authors aim to provide exact examples in 2D.
method: They study a 2D quantum Z2 gauge model dual to a spin-1/2 XY model on bipartite graphs, identifying exact eigenstates with a tower structure as scars.
result: Exact QMBS are found in the XY model and, via duality, in the gauge model, demonstrating a versatile construction.
conclusion: This work provides new exact QMBS in 2D, with potential for extension to other higher-dimensional models.

title: Pseudo-Hermitian Magnon Dynamics
authors: Xi-Guang Wang And Jamal Berakdar
abstract: A defining quantity of a physical system is its energy which is represented by the Hamiltonian. In closed quantum mechanical or/and fully coherent wave-based systems the Hamiltonian is introduced as a Hermitian operator which ensures real energy spectrum and secures the decomposition of any state over a complete basis set that spans the space where states live. Pseudo-Hermitian, or PT symmetric, systems are a special class of non-Hermitian ones. They describe open systems but may still have real energy spectrum. The eigenmodes are however not orthogonal in general. This qualitative difference to Hermitian physics has a range of consequences for the physical behavior of the system in the steady state or when it is subjected to external perturbations. This overview reviews the recent progress in the field of pseudo-Hermitian physics as it unfolds when applied to low-energy excitations of magnetically ordered materials. The focus is mainly on long wavelength spin excitations (spin waves) with magnons being the energy quanta of these excitations. Various setups including ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, magnonic crystals, and hybrid structures with different types of coupling to the environments as well as spatio-temporally engineered systems will be discussed with a focus on the particular aspects that are brought about by the pseudo-Hermiticity such as mode amplification, non-reciprocal propagation, magnon cloaking, non-Hermitian skin effect, PT-symmetric assisted Floquet engineering, topological energy transfer, and field-induced enhanced sensitivity.
tldr: A review of pseudo-Hermitian magnon dynamics in magnetically ordered materials, focusing on non-Hermitian effects such as mode amplification and non-reciprocal propagation.
motivation: To understand how pseudo-Hermiticity (PT symmetry) modifies the behavior of magnons in various magnetic systems, potentially enabling new functionalities.
method: The paper reviews theoretical and experimental progress on pseudo-Hermitian magnonics, covering ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, magnonic crystals, and hybrid structures.
result: Pseudo-Hermitian magnon systems exhibit unique phenomena like non-reciprocal propagation, magnon cloaking, non-Hermitian skin effect, and enhanced sensitivity.
conclusion: Pseudo-Hermitian magnonics is a rapidly developing field with potential applications in signal processing and sensing, but it is not directly aligned with the user's core interests in quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Complexity Of Graph-state Preparation By Clifford Circuits
authors: Soh Kumabe, Ryuhei Mori, And Yusei Yoshimura
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2165 (2026).

In this work, we study the complexity of graph-state preparation in a general model of quantum algorithms that allows measurements in the computational basis, single-qubit Clifford operations, and two-qubit Clifford operations. We define the CZ-complexity of a graph state [MATH] as the minimum number of two-qubit Clifford operations required to generate [MATH] from [MATH] for some [MATH]. Equivalently, every optimal algorithm can be taken to use only controlled-Z (CZ) gates as its two-qubit Clifford operations. We then give a combinatorial characterization of graph-state transformations. Specifically, [MATH] can be generated from another graph state [MATH] by an algorithm of CZ-complexity at most [MATH] if and only if [MATH] can be obtained from [MATH] by vertex deletions, local complementations and at most [MATH] elementary edge-complementations.
